1.pericope_label: Then David said, This is the house of the Lord God, and this is the altar of the burnt offering for Israel. And David commanded to gather together the strangers that were in the land of Israel; and he set masons to hew wrought stones to build the house of God. And David prepared iron in abundance for the nails for the doors of the gates, and for the joinings; and brass in abundance without weight; Also cedar trees in abundance: for the Zidonians and they of Tyre brought much cedar wood to David. And David said, Solomon my son is young and tender, and the house that is to be builded for the Lord must be exceeding magnifical, of fame and of glory throughout all countries: I will therefore now make preparation for it. So David prepared abundantly before his death.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the strangers as resident foreigners, the Canaanite population who lived on sufferance under Israelite dominion and were liable to forced service if the government required it, noting that Solomon afterwards found them by census to be a hundred and fifty-three thousand six hundred souls and that what originated with David was the organisation of the serf labour rather than the building itself. He shows that the word rendered young cannot fix Solomon's age, being vaguer than the Latin adolescens and ranging from a new-born babe to a man in the prime of life, and applied to Rehoboam at forty-one. On the quantities he is cool where the others are not, calling the iron and brass without weight a natural hyperbole and the cedars without number a rhetorical exaggeration, since the actual amounts would be known to the royal treasurers, and comparing the Assyrian habit of reckoning spoils without number. He also sees that the whole narrative of the census and the pestilence has its goal here, and that the chronicler would probably have omitted it, as he omitted the famine, but that it shows how the temple site was determined. Delitzsch adds that the Sidonians and Tyrians are named to denote the Phoenicians generally.

Gill agrees that the strangers were proselytes of the gate who had submitted to the precepts of Noah, and gives two reasons for using them, partly that they were better artificers than the Israelites, who were chiefly employed in husbandry and cattle, and partly that the Israelites, being freemen, might not be put to hard service; on Solomon's age he reports Jarchi's supposition of twelve while noting that the same word is used of Joshua at forty-two, and concludes that Solomon was probably about twenty.

Clarke takes the strangers for men who had become proselytes, at least so far as to renounce idolatry and keep the seven Noahic precepts, and says they were employed in the more servile and difficult parts of the work; on the site he is practical, holding that until a temple was built this place was to be considered the temple of God, and that on this altar and not the one at Gibeon the burnt offerings of Israel were to be made.

Henry draws David's motive from the description of Solomon, that being young and tender he was not likely to apply with great vigour at first and unless he found the wheels already turning would lose time, whereas with the materials ready to his hand the most difficult part would be over; those who are aged and experienced, Henry adds, should provide what help they can for the young. On the site he reads the ground pertaining to a Jebusite as a happy presage of the gospel temple set up among the Gentiles, and the threshing-floor as a figure of the church, which is God's floor and his threshing; this is the house, he says, because this is the altar, since the temple was built for the sake of the altar and there were altars long before temples.

debates: Who the strangers set to the work were, and so whether the temple was built by volunteers or by conscripts: Ellicott makes them Canaanite serfs liable to forced service, while Clarke and Gill make them religious proselytes who had taken on the Noahic precepts.

How old Solomon was, where Ellicott shows the word cannot settle it, since it ranges from a new-born babe to a man in his prime and is used of Rehoboam at forty-one, and Gill reports Jarchi at twelve before concluding for about twenty.

Whether the quantities are to be taken literally, which Ellicott treats as hyperbole and rhetorical exaggeration against the plain reading, observing that the royal treasurers would of course have known the actual amounts.
outliers: Ellicott holds that the chronicler kept the narrative of the census and the pestilence, which he would otherwise have omitted as he omitted the famine, only because it shows how the site of the temple was determined.
Gill gives as one reason for employing the strangers that they were simply better artificers than Israelites, who were chiefly occupied with husbandry and cattle.

6.pericope_label: Then he called for Solomon his son, and charged him to build an house for the Lord God of Israel. And David said to Solomon, My son, as for me, it was in my mind to build an house unto the name of the Lord my God: But the word of the Lord came to me, saying, Thou hast shed blood abundantly, and hast made great wars: thou shalt not build an house unto my name, because thou hast shed much blood upon the earth in my sight. Behold, a son shall be born to thee, who shall be a man of rest; and I will give him rest from all his enemies round about: for his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quietness unto Israel in his days. He shall build an house for my name; and he shall be my son, and I will be his father; and I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel for ever. Now, my son, the Lord be with thee; and prosper thou, and build the house of the Lord thy God, as he hath said of thee. Only the Lord give thee wisdom and understanding, and give thee charge concerning Israel, that thou mayest keep the law of the Lord thy God. Then shalt thou prosper, if thou takest heed to fulfil the statutes and judgments which the Lord charged Moses with concerning Israel: be strong, and of good courage; dread not, nor be dismayed. Now, behold, in my trouble I have prepared for the house of the Lord an hundred thousand talents of gold, and a thousand thousand talents of silver; and of brass and iron without weight; for it is in abundance: timber also and stone have I prepared; and thou mayest add thereto. Moreover there are workmen with thee in abundance, hewers and workers of stone and timber, and all manner of cunning men for every manner of work. Of the gold, the silver, and the brass, and the iron, there is no number. Arise therefore, and be doing, and the Lord be with thee.

schools.summary: Ellicott pronounces the dying address an ideal composition on grounds of internal evidence, put into the king's mouth by the unknown author whose work the chronicler follows or rather perhaps by the chronicler himself, whose style is evident throughout, and he compares the addresses attributed to David later in the book and the echoes he hears of the dying charge in Kings. On the bar he would render the charge literally as torrents of blood shed earthward and thinks the author may have remembered the charge against the shedder of man's blood in Genesis, but he points out that the oracle Nathan delivered promises success in war without any hint that warfare as such would unfit David, and that in Kings Solomon implies rather that his father's wars left him no leisure. He renders the charge's key phrases as wishes rather than commands, insists that obedience was an indispensable condition of the promise being fully realised while holding that the word of the Lord did not return void when the earthly dynasty ended, and defends the prayer for divine ratification against the charge of superfluity.
Gill reports the Targum turning the blessing on Solomon into a prayer that the Word of the Lord may be his help.

Clarke generalises the principle furthest, observing that heathens, Jews and Christians have all agreed that soldiers of any kind should have nothing to do with divine offices, the shedding of human blood ill comporting with the benevolence of God, and he illustrates it from the flight out of Troy, where the hero, just come from slaughter, would not handle the household gods himself but confided them to his father, holding it impious to touch holy things while red with new blood until he had washed in some living stream.

Henry dismisses the suggestion that the blood meant is Uriah's, since the honour was forbidden before that blood was shed, and concludes it must be the blood of David's wars, which though shed justly and honourably still made him less fit for this service than one never called to such work; from that he draws two inferences, that God showed how precious human life is to him and that he intended a type of the builder of the gospel temple, who should build not by destroying men's lives but by saving them. He reads the appointment as the ground of courage, since nothing is more powerful to engage us in any service for God than to know that hereunto we are appointed, and takes the promised rest as the opportunity rather than the reward, since where God gives rest he expects work.

debates: Whether the speech is David's own, which Ellicott denies on grounds of internal evidence, taking it for an ideal composition in the chronicler's own style, while the other voices expound it as the king's words.

Why David was barred from building, where the sources Ellicott sets side by side give three accounts - bloodshed here, no such reason at all in Nathan's oracle, and want of leisure in Kings - and where Henry rejects the reading that makes the blood Uriah's.

How far the promise to Solomon was conditional, which Ellicott holds was made quite clear by the verse on prospering, adding that the word of the Lord did not return void when the dynasty ended through disobedience.
outliers: Clarke holds that heathens, Jews and Christians have all agreed that soldiers should have nothing to do with divine offices, and illustrates it from a hero of pagan epic who would not touch holy things while red from slaughter.
Ellicott notes that the Hebrew reads his son where the margin and the versions rightly give my son, probably an oversight carried from the preceding verse.

17.pericope_label: David also commanded all the princes of Israel to help Solomon his son, saying, Is not the Lord your God with you? and hath he not given you rest on every side? for he hath given the inhabitants of the land into mine hand; and the land is subdued before the Lord, and before his people. Now set your heart and your soul to seek the Lord your God; arise therefore, and build ye the sanctuary of the Lord God, to bring the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and the holy vessels of God, into the house that is to be built to the name of the Lord.

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the same connection grammatically rather than devotionally, rendering the command as arise ye and build and holding that the second clause explains how the first was to be carried out, so that building the Lord a fair and noble sanctuary was equivalent to seeking his favour, with the comment that professions cost nothing and they were not to serve the Lord without cost. He notes that the phrase is to seek unto the Lord, the later construction where the older books use a simple accusative, that the word saying is absent from the Hebrew text as at several other places in this book, and that the second clause of the preceding question is better read as a statement that he has given you rest; the inhabitants given into David's hand he takes for the surrounding peoples whose reduction the earlier chapters describe, the chronicler thinking of the language of Numbers and Joshua about a land subdued before the Lord.

Gill reads the opening question as a reference to the wealth and riches with which God had blessed them, and takes the charge to seek God as meaning his honour and glory, sought most sincerely and cordially and to the utmost of their power.

Clarke supplies the political reckoning and turns it into a lament: David was by this time not only king of Judea but had subdued most of the surrounding nations, so that Solomon came to the throne with every possible advantage, and had he made proper use of his state and of his talents he would have been the greatest as well as the wisest of sovereigns; but alas, how soon did this pure gold become dim. He traces the decline in order, from an unlawful matrimonial connection to a commerce positively forbidden by the law of God and then to the multiplying of connections with heathen women who turned his heart away; and he quotes the Targum again for the opening question, which it turns into an assurance that the Word of the Lord is their assistant.

Henry makes the charge to the princes a point about how work gets done, since those who are in the throne cannot do the good they would unless those about the throne set in with them, so that David wanted the princes to advise Solomon and quicken him and make the work as easy to him as they could, each promoting it in his own place. He finds their obligation in gratitude for victory and rest and a good land, the more God has done for us being the more we should study to do for him; he presses the appeal to the heart, that they should place their happiness in God's favour and keep their eye on his glory, since where the heart is sincerely engaged the head and hand and estate and interest will all be cheerfully employed; and he closes with an encouragement for those who see little result, that much good may appear after our death which we never thought of.

debates: What seeking the Lord means in this charge, which Ellicott makes equivalent to the building itself, since the second clause explains how the first was to be carried out, while Henry makes it an inward disposition from which the outward work follows.

How the opening question should be read, where Ellicott would drop the interrogative in the second clause and take it as the statement that he has given you rest, while Clarke and Gill keep the question and answer it from the Targum and from the nation's prosperity.

What Solomon made of the advantage he inherited, which Clarke raises here and answers against him, holding that one who came to the throne with every possible advantage would have been the greatest of sovereigns had he used his state and talents properly.
outliers: Henry encourages those who see little fruit of their labour with the thought that much good may appear after our death which we never thought of, so that we should not be weary of well doing.
Ellicott observes that professions cost nothing, and that the princes were not to serve the Lord without cost.
